condition_entries.name: Acute vomiting, isolated episode

red_flags.description: Puppy or senior dog, or a dog with a known chronic illness
Repeated vomiting, three or more times in a few hours
Blood in the vomit
Swollen or distended abdomen with unproductive retching
Known or suspected access to toxins, a foreign object, or chocolate
Vomiting alongside lethargy, not drinking, or refusing food beyond one missed meal

condition_entries.home_care_guidance: For a single vomiting episode in an otherwise well adult dog: withhold food for a few hours (not water), then offer small, frequent amounts of a bland diet such as boiled chicken and white rice. Reintroduce normal food gradually over a few days once appetite and stools are back to normal.
condition_entries.prevention_tips: Secure bins and human food, and introduce new foods gradually over 7-10 days rather than all at once.

condition_entries.name: Occasional hairballs

red_flags.description: Hairballs more often than once or twice a month
Retching repeatedly without producing a hairball
Hairball vomiting alongside appetite loss, lethargy, diarrhea, or constipation
Blood in the vomit, or an unusually large, frothy, or discoloured hairball
A bloated or hard abdomen, or inability to keep food or water down

condition_entries.home_care_guidance: An occasional hairball (roughly once a month or less) in a cat who is otherwise eating, drinking, and behaving normally is generally nothing to worry about. Regular brushing reduces how much loose hair they swallow while grooming.
condition_entries.prevention_tips: Brush your cat regularly, especially long-haired breeds, and ask your vet about a hairball-control diet or fibre supplement if they're frequent.

condition_entries.name: Mild acute diarrhea, otherwise well

red_flags.description: Puppy or kitten, senior pet, or a pet with a known chronic illness
Blood in the stool, or black/tarry stool
Vomiting alongside the diarrhea
Lethargy, refusing food or water, or signs of dehydration such as dry gums or sunken eyes
Abdominal pain, bloating, or fever
Diarrhea lasting more than 24-48 hours despite home care

condition_entries.home_care_guidance: For a mild, isolated episode in an otherwise well adult pet: withhold food for 12-24 hours (fresh water always available), then reintroduce a bland diet such as boiled chicken or low-fat hamburger with white rice, in small frequent meals. This bland diet isn't nutritionally balanced long-term — transition back to normal food gradually over a few days once stools firm up.
condition_entries.prevention_tips: Introduce new foods gradually over 7-10 days, avoid rich table scraps, and keep parasite prevention up to date.

condition_entries.name: Reverse sneezing episode

red_flags.description: Episode lasts longer than 1-2 minutes, or doesn't fully resolve
Episodes becoming more frequent or severe
Nasal discharge or bloody discharge
Collapse, blue or grey gums/tongue, or struggling to breathe even outside the episode

condition_entries.home_care_guidance: Reverse sneezing (a rapid, repeated snorting or honking inhale) looks alarming but is usually a brief, harmless reflex from throat/soft-palate irritation. Stay calm — panicking tends to prolong it. Gently stroking the throat or briefly covering the nostrils to encourage a swallow can help end an episode sooner. It typically resolves in well under a minute with no lasting effect.
condition_entries.prevention_tips: Reduce exposure to dust, strong perfumes, and other airborne irritants. It's more common in small and brachycephalic breeds due to airway anatomy and isn't generally preventable beyond that.

condition_entries.name: Early, mild hot spot (acute moist dermatitis)

red_flags.description: The area is painful to touch, or your dog won't let you examine it
Increasing in size or depth despite home care
Discharge, pus, a foul smell, or persistent bleeding
No improvement within 1-2 days of starting home care
Fever or lethargy alongside the skin lesion

condition_entries.home_care_guidance: If the spot is small, non-painful, and caught early: gently trim (clippers, not scissors) the fur around it so air reaches the skin, clean gently with a dilute, pet-safe antiseptic — never hydrogen peroxide or alcohol, which damage tissue — and prevent licking with a cone if needed. Leave it uncovered; it needs to stay dry, not bandaged. Never use human topical ointments — some common ingredients like zinc oxide are toxic to dogs.
condition_entries.prevention_tips: Keep flea/parasite prevention current (a flea bite is a common trigger), and address matting or trapped moisture in thick coats promptly.

condition_entries.name: Minor cut or scrape

red_flags.description: Any bite wound, even a small one, has a high infection risk regardless of size
Bleeding doesn't stop after about 10-15 minutes of firm, continuous pressure
The wound is deep, over roughly 1cm long, or exposes fat, muscle, or bone
Wound near a joint or on the face
Signs of infection develop: redness, swelling, pus, odor, warmth, or your pet seems unwell
Heavy or uncontrolled bleeding, pale gums, or weakness

condition_entries.home_care_guidance: For a small, shallow scrape or cut with only minor bleeding: apply gentle, steady pressure with a clean cloth until bleeding stops, then rinse with clean water (skip strong antiseptics and any human ointment). Keep your pet from licking it — a recovery cone helps — and check it daily for the next few days for signs of infection.
condition_entries.prevention_tips: Supervised outdoor time and trimmed nails reduce injury risk; in multi-pet households, separate pets during high-arousal play or feeding to reduce fight-related bite wounds.

condition_entries.name: Mild flea infestation

red_flags.description: Puppy, kitten, senior, or a small/frail pet showing pale gums, weakness, or lethargy (possible flea-related anaemia)
Widespread hair loss, broken skin, or signs of a significant allergic reaction (flea allergy dermatitis)
Accidental exposure of a cat to a dog flea product or household flea spray containing permethrin

condition_entries.home_care_guidance: Comb your pet with a fine-toothed flea comb, and use a vet-recommended, species-appropriate flea treatment on every cat, dog (and rabbit) in the household on the same day. Most of a flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet, so wash bedding at 60°C+ and vacuum thoroughly, including furniture, to catch eggs and larvae too.
condition_entries.prevention_tips: Year-round vet-recommended flea prevention is far more effective than reactive treatment. CRITICAL: never use a dog flea product on a cat — many contain permethrin, which is highly toxic (potentially fatal) to cats.

condition_entries.name: Mild limping after exercise

red_flags.description: Puppy limping
Not putting any weight on the leg at all
Crying, yelping, or clear pain when the leg is touched
Visible swelling, heat, an open wound, or the leg looks bent or out of place
Follows a fall, being hit by a car, or other significant trauma
No improvement after 24-48 hours of rest, or the limp is recurring
Lethargy, not eating, or generally unwell alongside the limp

condition_entries.home_care_guidance: If your dog is still bearing some weight, shows no pain when the leg is gently touched, and is otherwise eating and behaving normally: rest is the treatment. Keep walks to short, slow, on-lead toilet breaks only, avoid stairs and jumping, and don't let them run or play for 24-48 hours. Most mild strains improve noticeably within that window.
condition_entries.prevention_tips: Warm up before intense exercise and avoid sudden increases in activity level, especially in dogs who are out of condition.
